newsitem.title: FINLAND: MUCH AT STAKE IN FINNISH CONFIDENCE VOTE -NIINISTO.
newsitem.headline: MUCH AT STAKE IN FINNISH CONFIDENCE VOTE -NIINISTO.

text.p: A vote of confidence in Finland's government due in February will not be just about shop opening hours but will also test MPs' faith in policies waiting ahead, Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto said on Tuesday.
"The confidence vote is not only about the past," Niinisto wrote in a column in daily newspaper Turun Sanomat.
"It will also be a measure of how the government parties' parliamentary groups view the policies waiting ahead," he said.
Many issues with broad implications for the future were scheduled to be decided this year, he said.

"Finland's EMU-decision is likely to mature already this spring," Niinisto said, noting the government will give to parliament a report on the pros and cons for Finland of EMU membership compared with remaining outside.
Parliament is scheduled to vote early next year on the question of Finnish participation in the planned third phase of Europe's Economic and Monetary Union.
"In connection with next year's incomes settlement the continuity of the taxation policy will be tested," he said.
Collective bargaining talks are due late in the autumn. A current nation-wide low-pay-rise deal expires in February 1998.
Niinisto said last week that the conditions to lower income taxes further would improve if trade unions and employer organisations agreed on modest pay rises from February 1998 onward, too.

In the column, he also said conditions were at hand for the government to balance the state finances, but gave no details. In 1996, government net borrowing at 33.8 billion markka was well below earlier forecasts around 38 billion.
The 1997 state net borrowing requirement is set at 28.3 billion markka.

Looking back at parliament's autumn session marked by several votes against government proposals, Niinisto said there had been "clear mistrust" in government policy within the parliamentary groups of government parties.
"That is why it is now appropriate to put confidence to the test," he said.
One of the defeated bills was a proposal to allow retail stores to keep their doors open on Sundays, too.
After the December setback, Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen said the bill would be reintroduced and debated once parliament convenes in February for the spring session.
Lipponen said the issue would also be a vote of confidence in his government. The confidence vote will be the fifth since the five-party rainbow coalition took office in April 1995.

"Parliament can now either trust the ruling government or get a new government coalition even without new elections," Niinisto wrote. But he said he did not think the opposition Centre Party was eager to be in government without a new mandate from voters.

And all government parties were probably not too keen on early elections, he added in an indirect reference to the poor showing of three coalition parties -- Lipponen's Social Democratic Party (SDP), the Leftist Alliance and the Green Party -- in municipal elections in October.
